title: Book I: Miss Brooke — Chapter VII
paragraphs:
“Piacer e popone
Vuol la sua stagione.”
—_Italian Proverb_.

As one would expect, Mr. Casaubon spent much of these weeks at the Grange. Courtship interrupted work on his great project, the Key to all Mythologies, and naturally made him look forward all the more eagerly to courtship’s happy conclusion. Still, he had knowingly accepted the interruption. He had decided the time had come to adorn his life with the graces of a woman’s companionship, to brighten with feminine imagination the gloom that fatigue often spread over the intervals between scholarly labors, and to secure, at this summit of his life, the comfort of a woman’s care for his declining years. Accordingly he resolved to surrender to the current of feeling, and perhaps was surprised to discover what a shallow trickle it was. As baptism by immersion can only be symbolic in drought-stricken regions, he found that sprinkling was the nearest his stream could bring him to a plunge. He concluded that poets greatly exaggerated the power of male passion. Nevertheless, he was pleased by Miss Brooke’s fervent, submissive love, which promised to fulfill his most agreeable expectations of marriage. Once or twice he wondered whether some deficiency in Dorothea might explain the moderation of his surrender. But he could identify none, nor imagine a woman who would please him better. Clearly, then, he had no explanation left except the exaggerations handed down in human tradition.

“Couldn’t I start preparing now to be more useful?” Dorothea asked him one morning early in their engagement. “Could I learn to read Latin and Greek aloud to you, like Milton’s daughters reading to their father without understanding the words?”

“I fear you would find it tiring,” Mr. Casaubon answered with a smile. “Indeed, if I recall correctly, the young women you mention considered this exercise in unfamiliar languages a reason to rebel against the poet.”

“Yes, but first they were very naughty girls, or they’d have been proud to serve such a father. And second, they could have studied privately and taught themselves to understand what they read. Then it would have interested them. I hope you don’t expect me to be naughty and stupid?”

“I expect you to be everything an exquisite young lady can be in every possible relation of life. Certainly your ability to copy Greek letters could be very useful. With that purpose, beginning with a little reading would be advisable.”

Dorothea seized on this permission as a precious gift. She would not have immediately asked him to teach her the languages, fearing above all to be a burden rather than a help. But devotion to her future husband was not her sole reason for wanting Latin and Greek. These territories of male knowledge seemed to offer a vantage point from which every truth could be seen more truly. As things stood, awareness of her ignorance made her constantly question her own conclusions. How could she be sure that one-room cottages did not glorify God, when men who knew the classics appeared able to combine indifference to cottages with zeal for that glory? Perhaps even Hebrew was necessary—at least its alphabet and a few roots—to get to the heart of things and judge a Christian’s social duties correctly. She had not yet reached the degree of self-renunciation at which having a wise husband would satisfy her. Poor child, she wanted to be wise herself. For all her supposed cleverness, Miss Brooke was certainly naive. Celia, whose mind nobody considered particularly powerful, recognized the emptiness of other people’s pretensions far more readily. Feeling little in general seems the only safeguard against feeling too much on any particular occasion.

Nevertheless, Mr. Casaubon agreed to spend an hour at a time listening and teaching, like a schoolmaster with small boys—or rather like a lover, to whom his beloved’s elementary ignorance and difficulties seem touchingly appropriate. Few scholars would have objected to teaching the alphabet in such circumstances. Dorothea herself, however, felt somewhat shocked and discouraged by her own slowness. The answers to her timid questions about the purpose of Greek accents raised a painful suspicion that this subject might indeed contain secrets beyond a woman’s powers of understanding.
On that point Mr. Brooke had no doubts. One day, entering the library during a reading lesson, he expressed himself with his customary force.
“Well, but Casaubon, deep studies like this—classics, mathematics and all that—strain a woman too much. Too much of a strain, you know.”
“Dorothea is only learning to read the letters,” Mr. Casaubon said, avoiding the issue. “She very thoughtfully proposed to spare my eyes.”

“Ah, well, without understanding, you know—that might not be so bad. But the feminine mind has a lightness, a touch-and-go quality. Music, the fine arts, that sort of thing—women should study those up to a point, but lightly, you know. A woman ought to be able to sit down and play or sing you a fine old English tune. That’s what I like, though I’ve heard most things. Been to the opera in Vienna: Gluck, Mozart, everything of that sort. But I’m conservative about music. It isn’t like ideas, you know. I stay with the good old tunes.”

“Mr. Casaubon doesn’t like the piano, and I’m very glad of it,” said Dorothea. Her low opinion of domestic music and ladies’ fine arts deserves forgiveness when we consider the faint tinkling and daubing that chiefly made them up in that dark age. She smiled gratefully up at her fiancé. Had he kept asking her to play “The Last Rose of Summer,” she would have needed great resignation. “He says there’s only an old harpsichord at Lowick, and it’s covered in books.”

“Ah, my dear, there Celia has the advantage. She plays very prettily and is always willing. Still, if Casaubon doesn’t like it, you’re all right. But it’s a pity to lack these little recreations, Casaubon. Keeping the bow strung all the time—that sort of thing, you know—won’t do.”

“I have never found recreation in having my ears tormented by rhythmic noises,” Mr. Casaubon said. “A frequently repeated tune has the absurd effect of forcing the words in my mind into a kind of minuet to keep time. After boyhood, I imagine, such an effect is barely tolerable. I say nothing of the grander forms of music, worthy of accompanying solemn ceremonies and even, in the ancient conception, of exercising an educational influence. Those do not immediately concern us here.”
“No, but I would enjoy music of that kind,” Dorothea said. “On our way home from Lausanne, uncle took us to hear the great organ at Freiberg, and it made me sob.”
“That isn’t healthy, my dear,” Mr. Brooke said. “Casaubon, she’ll be in your hands now. You must teach my niece to take things more calmly. Eh, Dorothea?”
He ended with a smile, not wanting to hurt her. He did think, though, that since she refused to consider Chettam, perhaps an early marriage to someone as sober as Casaubon was best.

“Remarkable, all the same,” he told himself as he shuffled out. “Remarkable that she should have liked him. But it’s a good match. I’d have exceeded my responsibilities by preventing it, whatever Mrs. Cadwallader says. Casaubon is almost certain to become a bishop. That pamphlet of his on the Catholic Question came at just the right moment. A deanery, at least. They owe him a deanery.”

Here I must establish my claim to philosophical reflection by observing that Mr. Brooke, on this occasion, little imagined the Radical speech he would later be led to make about bishops’ incomes. What elegant historian would miss a striking opportunity to point out that his heroes failed to foresee world history, or even their own actions? For instance, that Henry of Navarre, as a Protestant infant, scarcely thought of becoming a Catholic king; or that Alfred the Great, timing his laborious nights with burning candles, never imagined future gentlemen measuring their idle days with watches. Here is a mine of truth which, however vigorously excavated, will probably outlast our coal.

But I will add something about Mr. Brooke with perhaps less historical precedent: even if he had foreseen his speech, it might have made little difference. Enjoying the thought of his niece’s husband drawing a large Church income was one thing; delivering a Liberal speech was another. A mind that cannot view a subject from several angles is a narrow one.
